facts/ask: A build tool has to be told things. What is this program called? Which version? Where is its source?
facts/facts: Put together, a package is a bundle of named facts.
facts/compute: And the facts are connected. The file name repeats the version, and other packages will need this one. Fixed text cannot say that, so Nix has a small language of its own.
facts/set: Its main shape is the attribute set: names, each bound to a value, between curly braces. Nix evaluates an expression like this, which means it works out its value.
facts/semi: A semicolon ends every binding, the last one too. Leave one out and Nix stops with a syntax error.
facts/dot: A dot selects one value. dot version gives two point one two, and the comment underneath shows what Nix printed.
reach/nest: A value can be another set. Packages keep their extra facts in one, usually called meta.
reach/sugar: A dotted name on the left is shorthand for that nesting. Write meta dot license, and Nix builds the inner set for you.
reach/walk: Selection walks the same path, one dot at a time.
reach/miss: Ask for a name that is not there, and evaluation stops with an error.
reach/or: The word or gives a fallback instead. If the name is missing, you get what comes after it.
reach/has: A question mark only asks: is this name in the set? You get true or false.
merge/over: Often you want the same package with one fact changed: hello, at a newer version.
merge/update: The double slash operator merges two sets: the whole left one, with the right one laid over it.
merge/wins: A name that is on both sides takes the value from the right. Names on only one side come through unchanged.
merge/top: But only the top level merges. Meta is one name here, so the right side's meta replaces the left side's meta whole.
merge/gone: Nothing went inside to combine them, and the license is gone.
merge/names: A set has no order of its own. built-ins dot attr names lists its names sorted, whatever order you wrote them in.
share/repeat: Back to that file name. It repeats the version, so changing one means remembering the other.
share/plain: You might try to use the version right there. In a plain set, it fails: bindings cannot see each other.
share/rec: Put the word reck in front, short for recursive, and every binding can see every other.
share/inherit: Meta wants a version field with the same value. Inherit version copies that name in from around it, so you skip writing version equals version.
share/out: What comes out is an ordinary set of facts, and the version is now written in one place.
